r = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')

 texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n\\n'+text)
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:3]))

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: assessing degrees of human informational contribution in AI-assisted writing beyond binary human-versus-machine classification. The limitations appropriately distinguish informational contribution from creativity and legal authorship.

The experiments cover four domains, six generation models, repeated generations, and surrogate scoring models. The consistent ordering across polishing, summary-based generation, and less informative prompts provides credible evidence that the score captures a useful coarse signal.

The 1,500-pair human evaluation, with three annotators and 91.47% unanimous agreement, and the WildChat analysis provide useful additional evidence. The appendices document dataset sources, prompt templates, model versions, and threshold calibration, supporting partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central information-theoretic interpretation needs justification (Section 4.1). Equation 5 computes a pointwise log-likelihood ratio, not Shannon mutual information. Moreover, no distribution over prompts establishes that the no-input probability p(y) is the corresponding marginal. The normalized score can be negative even when the input is known. Predictive improvement from conditioning on a prompt does not, by itself, establish a proportion of information attributable to the human. This affects the central measurement claim, beyond a terminology correction.

The output-only derivation establishes a bound under a chosen plausibility criterion, but does not establish the minimum defined in Definition 2 (Appendix B). There is no demonstration that a feasible prompt attains or approaches the bound used in Equation 10. The mean-plus-one-standard-deviation calibration in Appendix A.5 also lacks held-out coverage and sensitivity analysis. Because paired inputs are available, the paper could directly measure how frequently the estimated lower bound exceeds the corresponding input-aware score.

For a fixed model and threshold, Equation 10 is exactly 1-c/h(y), where c=-log(tau) and h(y)=-log p(y)/N. It therefore produces the same rankings as ordinary perplexity. The detection AUCs and output-only pairwise agreement cannot distinguish the proposed interpretation from a perplexity-based detector. More generally, comparisons against input/output length ratios, lexical or semantic overlap, and likelihood components are missing, leaving unclear what the framework adds beyond simpler signals.

The human evaluation is selected using the metric being evaluated: only pairs with a measured gap greater than 0.1 are annotated (Section 5.1). Consequently, the reported 95.93% and 92.87% agreement rates characterize this selected population, not general ranking accuracy. Unfiltered sampling, results within domains and generation modes, and uncertainty estimates are needed. Neither these pairwise judgments nor the broad generation categories validate numerical contribution percentages.

Several robustness and applicability claims exceed the evidence. WildChat task categories provide indirect expectations rather than independently assessed contribution labels. The two fixed attack instructions in Appendix C.3 offer limited evidence about adaptive manipulation. Likewise, generic requests to correct hallucinations in Appendix C.5 do not establish that factual corrections occurred or independently validate changes in human informational contribution.

Important implementation details remain unspecified: the unconditional context used with instruction-tuned models, chat formatting, special-token and output-boundary handling, and whether likelihoods incorporate generation temperature. These choices directly affect both scores and calibration. No implementation or generated-dataset release is identified. Together with the unresolved measurement and evaluation issues, these gaps warrant important revisions before a Findings recommendation; the concern is evidential soundness rather than subjective interest or technical novelty.
